chapter: Trombone technique, plunger mute and the California years
title: Growing up in a small segregated town with few records and no radio
summary: He was born in 1906 in a town of 10,000 with 500 black residents, heard few records and visiting bands, and envies the exposure kids have today.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: you know. Well New Orleans probably just had a lot -- had more opportunities for musicians because there -- (Simultaneous conversation).

Yeah, New Orleans is a big town. I came from one of these little towns. You know -- I came from a small town -- 10,000 people. And it was a sort of a segregated town, too, and that part too, so there was only 500 colored people there you know. So where am I going to play? Where -- you know. That's when I was -- I was born -- I mean when I was a kid -- 1906, that's a long while ago you know. And so the country wasn't completely settled good yet. You know.
Also you didn't have the -- the phonograph had just about come on the scene and -- (Simultaneous conversation)

Phonographs had just come out and only people with a lot of money could afford one. You know -- and they'd get a record -- a record would come out about once or twice a year -- a new record. So you played that one record you got all year long. You know what I mean? So, like today -- the kids got such a -- a chance. You know, if I could have heard the things that the guys can -- the kids can hear now -- see they got radio

and they've got television. They can see you doing it, you know. There's a difference than when I came along cause I'd never seen nobody doing nothing. You know. Now and then -- a band would come through the town so everybody would go to hear it. And I know I just loved to hear bands. So, that's the way that was.
They didn't have things like street parades and so on.
Now and then a minstrel show would come in town and they'd make a parade up the streets, you know, and they played their pieces like the Scott Joplin numbers you know.
Dat, dat, dat -- them things. And --
Well, there's a tremendous difference between being exposed to --

Yeah, there's a chance to hear anything. Boy, when I came along what would I give for this. It's like they say -- born 50 years too soon. But I'm happy to be born 50 years sooner than these kids and I wish I could stay and see the whole thing through. Which is about -- oh, a hundred million more years.
On the other hand, maybe, you know, this where you grew up and you more or less had to invent your own --
you know -- to sound like everybody -- too many things pulling at you.
Yeah. You got problems all right.
